Resurrection and the Life
rez-uh-REK-shun and the lyfe
noun
Greek hē anastasis kai hē zōē (G386 + G2222) — "the resurrection and the life"; Christ's fifth I AM saying in John, spoken to Martha before raising Lazarus (John 11:25).

See also: Resurrection and the Life

📖 Biblical Definition

Resurrection and the Life is Christ's fifth I AM saying, spoken to Martha just before He raised Lazarus from the dead (John 11:25): "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?" The saying is structured in two halves, addressing two categories of believers. (1) "He that believeth in me, THOUGH HE WERE DEAD, yet shall he live" — those who die before Christ's return shall be raised from the dead at His coming (the resurrection of the body, 1 Cor 15). (2) "Whosoever LIVETH AND BELIEVETH in me shall never die" — those alive at Christ's return shall never see death (1 Thess 4:17 — caught up to meet the Lord in the air). Christ then asks Martha point-blank: "BELIEVEST THOU THIS?" — making the application personal: this is not abstract eschatology; it is a question of trust in Christ's specific person and word. Martha confesses: "Yea, Lord: I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God, which should come into the world." Christ then proceeds to demonstrate the title concretely by calling Lazarus out of the tomb. The pattern is the gospel in miniature: Christ DECLARES the divine title; ASKS for faith from the believer; DEMONSTRATES the truth of the title in resurrection power. Christ does not just promise resurrection at the last day; He IS the resurrection — the personal source and ground of all resurrection life. Believers do not just receive resurrection FROM Him; they receive resurrection IN Him.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Christ's fifth I AM saying, spoken to Martha before raising Lazarus; Christ is not just the giver of resurrection life but the personal source and ground.

expand to see more

RESURRECTION AND THE LIFE, noun. Christ's fifth "I AM" saying in John, spoken to Martha at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:25). "I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die."

Two halves of the promise: dead-believers will be raised; living-believers will never die (cf. 1 Cor 15:51-54; 1 Thess 4:13-17).

📖 Key Scripture

John 11:25-26 — "Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this?"

John 11:43-44 — "And when he thus had spoken, he cried with a loud voice, Lazarus, come forth. And he that was dead came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes: and his face was bound about with a napkin. Jesus saith unto them, Loose him, and let him go."

1 Corinthians 15:21-22 — "For since by man came death, by man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive."

John 5:25-26 — "Verily, verily, I say unto you, The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God: and they that hear shall live. For as the Father hath life in himself; so hath he given to the Son to have life in himself."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Resurrection and the Life is corrupted when modernist theology spiritualizes the resurrection ("He rose in our hearts" / "Christ lives on in his followers") rather than affirming the bodily resurrection Christ explicitly promises, or when the personal-faith demand ("Believest thou this?") is replaced with universal default-saving.

expand to see more

Spiritualized-resurrection theology. Modernist liberal theology often reduces Christ's resurrection to symbolic affirmation — He rose in the disciples' hearts, His teaching lives on, his spirit endures. But Christ's I AM saying is concrete: he RAISED LAZARUS bodily from the tomb to demonstrate the title. The resurrection is bodily, public, demonstrable. The same Christ who raised Lazarus will raise His people bodily at His return (1 Cor 15). To spiritualize resurrection is to deny the canonical demonstration and to empty the title "Resurrection and the Life" of its meaning.

Default-universalism replacing personal faith. "Believest thou this?" is the personal application Christ explicitly demanded of Martha. The promise of resurrection-life is conditional: "He that BELIEVETH in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live." Modern universalist theology often softens this — perhaps everyone will eventually be saved regardless of present faith. But Christ's question is sharp: do YOU believe? The title is a personal call to trust, not an automatic universal benefit.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hē anastasis kai hē zōē (G386 + G2222) — the resurrection and the life; Christ's fifth I AM saying, at Lazarus's tomb.

expand to see more

Greek anastasis (G386) — resurrection; from ana (up) + histēmi (to stand)

Greek zōē (G2222) — life; the higher-quality life-as-such, often distinguished from bios (mere biological life)

Christ's fifth Johannine I AM saying (John 11:25), spoken to Martha at Lazarus's tomb before raising him

Two-fold promise: dead-believers raised at the last day; living-believers never die at the Second Coming

Usage

"I am the resurrection, and the life — Christ at Lazarus's tomb claimed the divine Name and then demonstrated it."

"Believest thou this? — Christ's personal demand of Martha; not abstract eschatology but a question of trust."

"Christ does not just GIVE resurrection life; He IS resurrection life; we receive it not FROM Him alone but IN Him."
